tables.caption: Preventive measures in ANC by risk condition: iron/folate for anaemia (60 mg iron + 400 mcg folic acid daily), calcium 1500 mg for pre-eclampsia, mebendazole 500 mg, malaria, HIV testing and ART, hepatitis B testing

body.t: Iron deficiency anaemia
Check the woman's supply of the prescribed dose of iron/folate and whether she is taking them regularly as advised. Ask about diet.

Start iron/folate supplements at the first contact. Give 3 months' supply of daily iron/folate (1 tablet = 60 mg iron + 400 mcg folic acid), to be taken daily by all pregnant women to prevent anaemia. Refill the supply of iron/folate at subsequent contacts.
Counsel on adherence to prevent anaemia.
Counsel on correct and consistent use, management of side effects, and appropriate iron-rich food intake including food preparation.
All scheduled contacts
Pre-eclampsia
All women are at risk of pre-eclampsia. Check the woman's supply of calcium tablets at each contact.

Dispense 1500 mg of elemental calcium. Give 1500 mg to every pregnant woman at risk of developing pre-eclampsia (multiple pregnancy, obesity, family history of pre-eclampsia, diabetes) from 20 weeks until delivery.
All scheduled contacts
Intestinal worms
Check when the woman last received a dose of mebendazole (if within the previous 6 months, wait until 6 months have passed).
Give mebendazole (500 mg) once during the second or third trimester of pregnancy to every woman.
Contact 2 at 20 weeks
Malaria
Check when the last dose of an antimalarial was given.

Counsel on use of bed nets.
Perform RDT if she has malaria symptoms and treat if positive.
All contacts
HIV
Check knowledge of HIV status and partner's status.

Counsel and offer HIV testing to HIV-negative women and those of unknown HIV status. If negative, retest as per schedule; encourage partner HIV testing. If positive and not on treatment, start ART (see National HIV integrated guidelines, PMTCT section).
Provide adherence and psychosocial support; if on ART provide support; encourage and emphasise the use of condoms and encourage VMMC.
All scheduled contacts
Hepatitis B
Check knowledge about hepatitis; history of blood transfusion, jaundice, contact/exposure to hepatitis B.
Test for hepatitis B; if positive, counsel and refer to the next level of care. If negative, counsel and repeat when the next HIV/syphilis screening is done.
1st contact

source_flags: Calcium: the assessment column says all women are at risk and 'dispense 1500 mg', but the treatment text limits calcium to women 'at risk of developing pre-eclampsia' (multiple pregnancy, obesity, family history, diabetes) from 20 weeks; the contact schedule lists calcium at every contact from contact 1.
'Elementary calcium' printed (elemental calcium); the calcium dose is not split (WHO: 1.5–2.0 g daily in divided doses).

tables.heading_path: 3.0 Providing ANC Services > 3.6 Preventive Measures > Tetanus-Diphtheria (Td) Vaccination
tables.caption: Td (tetanus-diphtheria) vaccination in pregnancy by prior TTCV doses: unknown/none, 3 or 4 childhood doses, later boosters – doses needed and intervals
tables.content:
If a pregnant woman received:
- No TTCV doses or unknown vaccination status → she will need: (a) 1 Td dose as early as possible; (b) 1 Td dose at least 4 weeks later; (c) 1 Td dose at least 6 months later; (d) 1 Td dose at least 1 year later; (e) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (to obtain long-term protection).
- Only 3 TTCV doses in childhood → (a) 1 Td dose at the first ANC visit; (b) another Td dose 4 weeks later (to be protected for that pregnancy); (c) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).
- 4 TTCV doses in childhood → (a) 1 Td dose at that visit (to be protected for that pregnancy); (b) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).
- 3 TTCV doses in childhood and 1 Td or 1 DT dose later → (a) 1 Td dose at that visit (to be protected for that pregnancy); (b) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).
- 4 TTCV doses in childhood and 1 Td dose later → 1 Td dose at that contact (no further doses required).
- 4 TTCV doses and 2 Td boosters → no vaccination; the woman is fully protected.
(TTCV = tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine.)

tables.heading_path: 6.0 Managing Complications of Pregnancy > 6.1 Vaginal Bleeding in Early Pregnancy > 6.1.2 Clinical Assessment
tables.caption: Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy: threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete and missed abortion, molar pregnancy, pregnancy of uncertain viability, pregnancy of unknown location – clinical assessment, ultrasound findings, management

body.t: Threatened abortion

- Light bleeding
- Abdominal pain
- Closed cervix
- Uterus corresponds to dates

- Intrauterine gestation sac
- Fetal pole
- Fetal heart activity

- Take vital signs: pulse, blood pressure; do pregnancy test and haemoglobin.
- Refer urgently to health centre or hospital.
- Ultrasound scan to be done at health centre or hospital.
Inevitable abortion

- Heavy bleeding
- Abdominal pain
- Opened cervix
- Uterus corresponds to dates
Intrauterine gestation sac ± fetal pole ± fetal activity

- Take vital signs: pulse, blood pressure; do pregnancy test and haemoglobin.
- Insert 2 large IV lines, run normal saline or Ringer's lactate, and relieve pain.
- Refer urgently to health centre or hospital.
- Ultrasound scan to be done at health centre or hospital.
Incomplete abortion

- Heavy bleeding with history of expulsion of products of conception
- Abdominal pain
- Uterus smaller than dates
- Opened cervix

- Heterogeneous tissues ± gestation sac
- Any endometrial thickness >15 mm

- Take vital signs: pulse, blood pressure; do pregnancy test and haemoglobin.
- Insert 2 large IV lines, run normal saline or Ringer's lactate, and relieve pain.
- Refer urgently to health centre or hospital.
- Ultrasound scan to be done at health centre or hospital.
- MVA should be done to evacuate the uterus by a trained health professional.
Complete abortion

- Bleeding and abdominal pain cease
- Cervix closed

- Empty uterus
- Endometrial thickness <15 mm
Ultrasound scan to be done at health centre or hospital.
Missed abortion / early fetal demise

- Bleeding
- Abdominal pain, loss of pregnancy symptoms
- Closed cervix

- Fetal pole >7 mm with no fetal heart activity
- Mean gestation sac diameter >25 mm with no fetal pole or yolk sac
Ultrasound scan to be done at health centre or hospital.
Molar pregnancy

- Heavy bleeding with history of expulsion of products of conception
- Abdominal pain
- Nausea and vomiting
- Opened cervix
- Uterus larger than dates
- Uterus softer than normal

- 'Snowstorm' appearance of mixed echogenicity
- ± Large theca lutein cysts
Ultrasound scan to be done at health centre or hospital. The uterus should be evacuated by a trained health professional and the client followed up stringently as per guidelines.
Pregnancy of uncertain viability

- ± bleeding ± pain
- Closed cervix

- Intrauterine gestation sac <25 mm with no fetal pole or yolk sac
- Fetal pole with CRL <7 mm with no fetal heart activity
Rescan in 1 week
Pregnancy of unknown location (PUL)

- ± bleeding ± pain
- Closed cervix

- Positive pregnancy test
- Empty uterus
- No sign of extrauterine pregnancy
Serial serum hCG assay (48 h apart). Rescan in 2 weeks.

source_flags: The abortion definition reads 'before 20 weeks' gestation or with a fetus born weighing 500 g' (presumably 'less than 500 g').
Missed abortion and molar pregnancy rows give only 'ultrasound at health centre or hospital' – no instruction to refer or on vital signs/IV access, unlike the other rows.
tables.table_note: NOTE: Tachycardia should be taken seriously even in a stable-looking patient.
tables.context_before: Abortion is defined as expulsion or extraction of a pregnancy before 20 weeks' gestation or a fetus weighing 500 g.

tables.heading_path: 6.0 Managing Complications of Pregnancy > 6.2 Ectopic Pregnancy > 6.2.2 Signs, Symptoms and Management
tables.caption: Ectopic pregnancy: symptoms (amenorrhoea, unilateral lower abdominal pain, spotting, shoulder tip pain, collapse), signs, and emergency management (IV lines, urgent referral)

body.t:
- Often asymptomatic (unsure of dates)
- Amenorrhoea (usually 6–8 weeks)
- Lower abdominal pain (classically unilateral)
- Vaginal bleeding (usually spotting and brown in colour)
- Diarrhoea and vomiting should not be ignored
- Dizziness and light-headedness
- Shoulder tip pain (diaphragmatic irritation – haemoperitoneum)
- Collapse (if ruptured)

- Often no specific signs
- Uterus usually normal size
- Cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness occasionally
- Adnexal mass very rare
- Confusion and restlessness
(Suspect ectopic pregnancy in any woman of reproductive age with a history of amenorrhoea and unilateral lower abdominal pain, tachycardia, dizziness, fainting.)

- Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure; do pregnancy test and haemoglobin. NOTE: tachycardia should be taken seriously even in a stable-looking patient.
- Insert 2 large-bore IV lines
- Run normal saline or Ringer's lactate
- Refer urgently to hospital
- Ultrasound scan must be done. This is an emergency and must be managed immediately!

tables.context_before: Ectopic pregnancy is implantation of the pregnancy outside the uterine cavity.

tables.heading_path: 6.0 Managing Complications of Pregnancy > 6.3 Antepartum Haemorrhage > 6.3.3 Diagnosis of Antepartum Haemorrhage
tables.caption: Antepartum haemorrhage: abruptio placentae vs placenta praevia vs ruptured uterus – signs and symptoms; general emergency management (ABC, IV lines, no digital vaginal examination, refer)

body.t: Abruptio placentae

- Vaginal bleeding
- Intermittent or constant abdominal pain
- Shock
- Tender, tense uterus
- Decreased or absent fetal movement
- Fetal distress or absent fetal heart sounds

General management:
Shout for help! (Inyandzaleyo!)
- Follow A, B, C: airway clear, breathing, circulation.
- Assess the haemodynamic status of the patient.
- Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure; do urgent ward Hb.
- NOTE: tachycardia should be taken seriously even in a stable-looking patient; also confusion and restlessness.
- Resuscitate as appropriate: insert 2 large IV lines; correct hypovolaemia using normal saline or Ringer's lactate; strict fluid balance chart, insert Foley's catheter, monitor input and output; if available give oxygen 4–6 L per minute by face mask; blood grouping and cross-match, FBC.
Refer the patient to hospital as soon as possible.
NOTE: DO NOT PERFORM DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION UNTIL PLACENTA PRAEVIA IS RULED OUT.
Placenta praevia

- Vaginal bleeding (painless, bright red), may be precipitated by intercourse
- Shock
- Relaxed uterus
- Fetal presentation not in the pelvis; malpresentation; lower uterine pole feels empty
- Normal fetal condition
Ruptured uterus

- Vaginal or intra-abdominal bleeding
- Severe abdominal pain (may decrease after rupture)
- Shock
- Abdominal distension or free fluid
- Abnormal uterine contour
- Tender abdomen
- Easily palpable fetal parts
- Absent fetal movement and fetal heart sounds
- Rapid maternal pulse

source_flags: Ruptured uterus sign printed 'Abdominal uterine contour' (abnormal uterine contour).
The general management is printed against abruptio placentae only; it is read here as applying to all three diagnoses.
tables.context_before: APH is bleeding from or into the genital tract from 28 weeks of pregnancy until before delivery of the baby. Any bleeding in a pregnant woman should be taken seriously. Spotting; minor haemorrhage <50 ml that has settled; major haemorrhage 50–1000 ml with no signs of shock; massive haemorrhage >1000 ml and/or signs of clinical shock.

tables.heading_path: 6.0 Managing Complications of Pregnancy > 6.5 Eclampsia > 6.5.2 Risk Factors and Symptoms
tables.caption: Eclampsia: risk factors, symptoms and emergency management of convulsions (left lateral, airway, oxygen, magnesium sulphate, urgent referral)

body.t:
- 1st pregnancy
- Age >40 years
- Overweight (BMI >35 at 1st ANC visit)
- Family history of PIH / pre-eclampsia
- Multiple pregnancy
- Last pregnancy >10 years ago
- Chronic kidney disease
- Diabetes mellitus
- Autoimmune diseases
- Race – black
- Chronic hypertension

- May be asymptomatic
- Headache not relieved by simple analgesia
- Altered mental state
- Blindness
- Shortness of breath
- Blurred vision or flashing
- Epigastric / right upper quadrant abdominal pain
- Rapid swelling of face, hands and feet
- Non-specific complaints of being unwell
- Convulsions

- Urgently refer the patient to the nearest hospital.
- Give a pre-referral loading dose of magnesium sulphate 4 g IM.
- For a patient with convulsions: do not leave the patient alone; shout for assistance, state 'Eclampsia'; turn the patient to the left lateral position; ensure the airway is clear and the patient is breathing; protect the patient from falling/injury; do not place anything in the mouth; oxygen by mask at 4–6 L per minute; when the convulsion ends, start IV; take vital signs.
- At the hospital, stabilise the patient and deliver by the safest, fastest route; manage eclampsia as per guidelines.

source_flags: Same magnesium sulphate '4 g IM' pre-referral dose as for severe pre-eclampsia (see above).
tables.context_before: Eclampsia: seizures that cannot be attributed to other causes in a woman with pre-eclampsia.

tables.heading_path: 6.0 Managing Complications of Pregnancy > 6.4 Pre-eclampsia > 6.4.2 Signs and Symptoms
tables.caption: Pre-eclampsia: mild (BP ≥140/90 twice 4 hours apart) vs severe (BP ≥160/110, proteinuria, headache, blurred vision, epigastric pain, oliguria, thrombocytopenia) – referral and pre-referral magnesium sulphate

body.t: Mild pre-eclampsia

- BP ≥140/90 on ≥2 occasions measured at least 4 hours apart, without evidence of end-organ damage, in women with previously normal BP before 20 weeks' gestation
OR
- An increase in systolic BP by 30 mmHg or diastolic BP by 15 mmHg
Refer the client to the regional referral hospital (if at the clinic, PHU). At the hospital, manage as per guidelines.
Severe pre-eclampsia: any 1 of the following in the presence of pre-eclampsia

- SBP ≥160 mmHg or DBP ≥110 mmHg
- Proteinuria >5 g in a 24-hour urine collection or 3+ on dipstick
- Pulmonary oedema / cyanosis
- Urine output <30 ml/hr (oliguria)
- Persistent headaches
- Blurred vision
- Epigastric pain ± impaired liver function
- Oligohydramnios
- Decreased fetal growth
- Placental abruption
- Thrombocytopenia

Refer the client to the regional referral hospital (if at the clinic, PHU). Give a pre-referral loading dose of magnesium sulphate 4 g IM if at the clinic or PHU. At the hospital, manage as per guidelines.

source_flags: Pre-referral magnesium sulphate is given as '4 g IM'. The WHO IM regimen is 4 g IV plus 10 g IM (5 g in each buttock), or 10 g IM where IV is not possible; 4 g IM alone is below standard loading doses. Clinician to confirm.
'Mild' pre-eclampsia still uses the older '30/15 mmHg rise' criterion, which is no longer used to define hypertension in pregnancy.
tables.context_before: Pre-eclampsia is new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks' gestation with significant proteinuria, with or without oedema; it can present as late as 4–6 weeks postpartum.

tables.heading_path: 6.0 Managing Complications of Pregnancy > 6.6 Premature Rupture of Membranes
tables.caption: Premature rupture of membranes (PROM) and preterm PROM (PPROM): assessment, clinic management (no digital vaginal exam, refer), hospital management by gestation (steroids betamethasone/dexamethasone, antibiotics erythromycin/amoxicillin, induction)

body.t: Premature rupture of membranes (PROM)

- Verify the patient's estimated due date; this will be needed for management decisions.
- Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure and temperature 4-hourly.
- Do urine dipstick.
- Check fetal heart rate.

- DO NOT perform digital vaginal examination.
- Refer to health centre or hospital.

- If term, this may indicate onset of labour.
- Assess for other signs of labour.
- Perform a sterile speculum examination to assess whether the cervix is open.
- Give antibiotics if prolonged rupture of membranes.
- Allow to deliver if in labour.
Preterm PROM (PPROM)

- Assess as indicated in PROM.
- Ultrasound at least twice a day.
- Consider weekly maternal FBC.

- DO NOT perform digital vaginal examination.
- Refer to health centre or hospital.

If rupture is:
- Before 28 weeks: observe vital signs; initiate the process of evacuation by stimulation after counselling the mother and significant others about the risks.
- Before 34 weeks (28–33 weeks): administer steroids – intramuscular betamethasone 12 mg every 12 hours for 24 hours, OR intramuscular dexamethasone.
- Regularly inspect the sanitary pad for the amount, colour and odour of the amniotic fluid.
- Strict bed rest.
- Oral erythromycin and amoxicillin (500 mg PO 6-hourly) should be given for 10 days following the diagnosis of PPROM.
PPROM >34 and <37 weeks, and PROM >37 weeks
Assess as indicated in PROM.
Refer to hospital (transfer is preferable while the baby is in utero).

- Give antibiotic prophylaxis within 8 hours.
- Give steroids before 37 weeks.
- If no evidence of fetal distress, leave the patient for up to 24 hours.
- If the patient does not go into labour within 24 hours, induce.
- Monitor labour normally.

source_flags: Betamethasone '12 mg every 12 hours for 24 hours' – the usual regimen is 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses; the dexamethasone dose is not given.
'Ultrasound at least twice a day' for PPROM is implausible (probably vital signs or fetal heart rate twice a day).
PPROM before 28 weeks: 'initiate process of evacuation by stimulation' – clinician to confirm intent.
The >34-week row says 'give steroids before 37 weeks', which conflicts with steroids being limited to 28–33 weeks above.
Erythromycin dose is not given; '500 mg PO 6-hourly' appears to apply to amoxicillin only.
tables.context_before: PROM is drainage of amniotic fluid through the cervical canal before the onset of uterine contractions; it may be preterm (before 37 weeks) or at term (after 37 weeks).

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Managing Common Conditions in Pregnancy > 7.1 Anaemia during Pregnancy > 7.1.3 Classification and Management
tables.caption: Anaemia in pregnancy by haemoglobin: no anaemia (>11 g/dl), moderate (7-11 g/dl: double-dose iron 3 months), severe (<7 g/dl: urgent referral) – clinic vs hospital management

body.t: >11 g/dl (no pallor)
No clinical anaemia
Give the usual daily dose of iron and folic acid and counsel on compliance. Provide counselling on nutrition.
Give the usual daily dose of iron and folic acid and counsel on compliance. Provide counselling on nutrition.
7–11 g/dl OR palmar and conjunctival pallor
Moderate anaemia

Give a double dose of daily iron for 3 months and counsel on compliance and nutrition (such as chuchuza, imbuya, spinach etc.); re-assess at the next ANC contact or sooner if danger signs occur. If haemoglobin [<]8 g/dl or symptoms occur (shortness of breath, dizziness), urgently refer to health centre or hospital.

Give a double dose of daily iron for 3 months and counsel on compliance and nutrition; re-assess at the next ANC contact or sooner. If symptoms occur, do further clinical and laboratory assessment and treat accordingly.
<7 g/dl and/or severe palmar and conjunctival pallor, OR any pallor with respirations [>]30/minute or breathlessness at rest
Severe anaemia
Refer urgently to health centre or hospital.
Conduct further clinical and laboratory assessment and treat accordingly. Counsel to give birth at a facility with transfusion capacity.

source_flags: 'If haemoglobin 8 g/dl' and 'respirations 30/minute' are printed without a comparison sign; read as <8 g/dl and >30/minute.
The table uses >11 g/dl for no anaemia, while the definition above uses <10.5 g/dl in the 2nd trimester; Hb 10.5–11 in the 2nd trimester falls in 'moderate anaemia' here.
'Double dose of daily iron' is not given in mg.
tables.context_before: Anaemia: Hb <11 g/dl in the 1st trimester, <10.5 g/dl in the 2nd trimester, <11 g/dl in the 3rd trimester. Symptoms are often non-specific (tiredness, weakness, headaches, palpitations, dizziness, dyspnoea).

### 3.7.4 Birth preparedness

Educate pregnant women about birth preparedness and jointly with the pregnant woman develop a birth preparedness plan including the following:
- Advise the woman to identify transport, and allocate money that will be required for travel and other expenses.
- Explain when she needs to go to the facility (Signs of true labour or if she has any complications).
- Advise on what to bring to the facility for herself and the baby such as: her maternal ANC record /card, clean cloths, towel for drying and wrapping the baby, nappies/diapers, baby blankets, Clean clothes for both the mother and the baby; toiletries including sanitary pads, toothbrush and paste, food and other supplies), carry a travel bag; Birth registration items (National ID card; copy of marriage certificate if married and the copy of father's ID), ultrasound scans, and any medication that she is taking.
- Review and update the Birth and Emergency Plan at each ANC contact

text_add.text:
## Foreword

The Global Strategy for Women's, Children's and Adolescent Health 2016 – 2030 prioritizes provision of quality health services to women, newborns, children and adolescents and acknowledges that investing more in their health contributes to the realization of their right to health. The Kingdom of Eswatini aligns itself with this global health and human rights commitment. The Kingdom's efforts in attaining the targets of the Sustainable Development Goals is operationalized through the Eswatini National Sustainable Development Strategy and the Health Sector Strategic plan. The Government of Eswatini has made significant progress in the provision of maternal, newborn and adolescent health. This is evident in the high ANC coverage (at least once at 98%), and institutional deliveries (87.7 %), skilled birth attendance (88%) MICS 2014 and postnatal Care coverage of 71% (SRH Annual report). However, there is a clinical gap in the provision of quality of care evidenced by an unacceptably high Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) at 593/100,000 live births (Intercensus Demographic Housing Survey, 2012) and Neonatal Mortality Ratio (NMR) at 20 per 1000 live births MICS 2014. In an effort to respond to the challenges, the MOH has developed the first national ANC guidelines which will improve provision of quality of health services, and implementation of the guidelines will contribute to the well-being of women and families and will further contribute to positive perinatal and maternal outcomes. The benefits of the guidelines are as follows:

## Foreword

- It is a platform to ensure timely and consistent health promotion, screening, diagnosis, disease prevention and management of complications in the context of respectful care.
- It also serves as a standard for quality health services.
- Through ANC activity (prevention, screening, diagnosis, management), this guideline will contribute to reducing MMR and incidence of still birth in the country.

These guidelines are in line with the new WHO ANC recommendations 2016 and are designed for use by all health care providers in the sector (Government, Private, NGOs) both at health facility and community levels. In this regard, all health workers providing ANC services are expected to adhere to these new guidelines. All partners and training institutions involved in-service and pre-service teaching should adjust their training to reflect this new guidance. The Ministry of Health is committed to ensure that the requisite resources are made available for the effective implementation of the guidelines.

## 3.0 Providing ANC Services

ANC services can start as soon as the woman misses a period and suspects that she is pregnant. The ANC services that are provided must be in line with the ANC service package outlined in this guideline.
